rules.title: Runs strings as code (eval)
rules.why: eval executes arbitrary text as code, which is the usual way to hide what a plugin really does from review.

rules.title: Builds functions from strings (new Function)
rules.why: Same risk as eval: code that does not exist in the file until it runs.

rules.title: Starts other programs (child_process)
rules.why: Lets a plugin run any program on the user's machine with the user's privileges, far outside what a note-taking plugin needs.

rules.title: Loads code chosen at runtime (dynamic require/import)
rules.why: A literal module name can be reviewed; a computed one can load anything, including code fetched later.

rules.title: Reaches into Electron internals
rules.why: Direct Electron access can bypass Obsidian's API boundaries (windows, shell, clipboard, OS integration).

rules.title: Uses native bindings (process.binding / .node addon)
rules.why: Native code cannot be reviewed as JavaScript.

rules.title: Uses Node file system directly
rules.why: Node fs can read and write outside the vault. Plugins should normally use Obsidian's vault API. Listed for a human to judge.

rules.title: Makes network requests
rules.why: Any network call can send vault content out. Many legitimate plugins do this; the referenced hosts are listed so a human can check them.

rules.title: Touches cookies or credential stores
rules.why: Reading cookies or the OS credential store is rarely needed by a plugin and is a common theft target.

rules.title: Looks obfuscated (large encoded blobs)
rules.why: Big encoded strings decoded at runtime are a standard way to hide a payload.
